sectionTitle: Using the Earth's resources and obtaining potable water

specStatements.text: Humans use the Earth’s resources to provide warmth, shelter, food and transport.
Natural resources, supplemented by agriculture, provide food, timber, clothing and fuels.
Finite resources from the Earth, oceans and atmosphere are processed to provide energy and materials.

Chemistry plays an important role in improving agricultural and industrial processes to provide new products and in sustainable development, which is development that meets the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
Students should be able to:
state examples of natural products that are supplemented or replaced by agricultural and synthetic products
distinguish between finite and renewable resources given appropriate information.
Students should be able to:
extract and interpret information about resources from charts, graphs and tables
use orders of magnitude to evaluate the significance of data.

Water of appropriate quality is essential for life. For humans, drinking water should have sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and microbes. Water that is safe to drink is called potable water. Potable water is not pure water in the chemical sense because it contains dissolved substances.
The methods used to produce potable water depend on available supplies of water and local conditions.
In the United Kingdom (UK), rain provides water with low levels of dissolved substances (fresh water) that collects in the ground and in lakes and rivers, and most potable water is produced by:
choosing an appropriate source of fresh water
passing the water through filter beds
sterilising.
Sterilising agents used for potable water include chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light.

If supplies of fresh water are limited, desalination of salty water or sea water may be required. Desalination can be done by distillation or by processes that use membranes such as reverse osmosis. These processes require large amounts of energy.
Students should be able to:
distinguish between potable water and pure water
describe the differences in treatment of ground water and salty water
give reasons for the steps used to produce potable water.
Required practical 8: analysis and purification of water samples from different sources, including pH, dissolved solids and distillation.

Urban lifestyles and industrial processes produce large amounts of waste water that require treatment before being released into the environment. Sewage and agricultural waste water require removal of organic matter and harmful microbes. Industrial waste water may require removal of organic matter and harmful chemicals.
Sewage treatment includes:
screening and grit removal
sedimentation to produce sewage sludge and effluent
anaerobic digestion of sewage sludge
aerobic biological treatment of effluent.
Students should be able to comment on the relative ease of obtaining potable water from waste, ground and salt water.
The Earth’s resources of metal ores are limited.

Copper ores are becoming scarce and new ways of extracting copper from low-grade ores include phytomining, and bioleaching. These methods avoid traditional mining methods of digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock.
Phytomining uses plants to absorb metal compounds. The plants are harvested and then burned to produce ash that contains metal compounds.
Bioleaching uses bacteria to produce leachate solutions that contain metal compounds.
The metal compounds can be processed to obtain the metal. For example, copper can be obtained from solutions of copper compounds by displacement using scrap iron or by electrolysis.
Students should be able to evaluate alternative biological methods of metal extraction, given appropriate information.

scopeNotes.statement: Desalination can be done by distillation or by processes that use membranes such as reverse osmosis. These processes require large amounts of energy.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only the two routes the specification names are taught - distillation, and membrane processes of which reverse osmosis is the given example - together with the single consequence the specification states, that they require large amounts of energy. Nothing is asked about osmotic pressure, membrane materials, operating pressures, multi-stage flash plants or costings, because the specification does not develop the processes beyond naming them.

scopeNotes.statement: Sterilising agents used for potable water include chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Questions ask only which agents are used and what sterilising achieves. No equation for chlorine in water, no mechanism for how ozone or ultraviolet light destroys microbes, and no comparison of dose rates is required, because the specification lists the three agents and stops there.

scopeNotes.statement: Required practical 8: analysis and purification of water samples from different sources, including pH, dissolved solids and distillation.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The practical is examined through the three named strands only: measuring pH, finding dissolved solids by evaporating a known volume to dryness, and purifying a sample by distillation. No named-ion tests, titrations or hardness determinations are introduced, because the specification lists exactly these three analyses.

scopeNotes.statement: Copper ores are becoming scarce and new ways of extracting copper from low-grade ores include phytomining, and bioleaching.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only the two named biological methods are taught, and only for copper from low-grade ores as the specification frames it. No named plant or bacterial species, no biochemistry of uptake and no other biological extraction route is required.

scopeNotes.statement: For example, copper can be obtained from solutions of copper compounds by displacement using scrap iron or by electrolysis.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The two processing routes named by the specification are taught to the depth already established elsewhere in the course - displacement follows the reactivity series, electrolysis deposits copper at the negative electrode. No electrode potentials, no purification-of-copper cell design and no yield calculations are added here.

concepts.definition: Anything taken from the Earth, the oceans or the atmosphere that people use. Humans use the Earth's resources to provide warmth, shelter, food and transport, and natural resources, supplemented by agriculture, provide food, timber, clothing and fuels.

A resource that is not being replaced, or is being replaced far more slowly than it is used, so the supply available on Earth will eventually run out. Crude oil, natural gas and metal ores are finite.
A resource that is replaced at the same rate as, or faster than, it is used, so it can be re-formed within a human lifetime. Timber from managed woodland and cotton are renewable.
Development that meets the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

A product made by an industrial chemical process rather than taken directly from a living thing, made to supplement or replace a natural product, for example synthetic rubber in place of latex from rubber trees.
A product obtained by deliberately farming plants or animals, which supplements the supply obtained from wild natural sources, for example farmed timber, wool and cotton.
A factor of ten. Two quantities differ by one order of magnitude if one is about ten times the other, and by three orders of magnitude if one is about a thousand times the other.
Water that is safe to drink. For humans, drinking water should have sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and microbes.
In the chemical sense, water containing only H2O and nothing else. Potable water is not pure water in the chemical sense because it contains dissolved substances.
Water with low levels of dissolved substances. In the UK rain provides fresh water that collects in the ground and in lakes and rivers.
Beds of sand and gravel that water is passed through during treatment so that insoluble solids and larger particles are removed.
Treating water so that microbes in it are killed, making the water safe to drink.
A treatment used to kill microbes in water. Sterilising agents used for potable water include chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light.
Removing dissolved salts from salty water or sea water so that it can be used as potable water. It may be required if supplies of fresh water are limited.
Boiling water and condensing the vapour, so that the water separates from the dissolved solids, which stay behind. One route to desalination and the purification step of Required practical 8.
A desalination process that forces salty water through a membrane which holds back the dissolved ions and lets water through.
Fresh water that has collected in the ground, one of the appropriate sources of fresh water chosen in the UK.
Water containing high levels of dissolved salts, such as sea water, which needs desalination rather than simple filtering and sterilising.
The solid substances dissolved in a water sample, found in Required practical 8 by evaporating a measured volume to dryness and weighing the residue.
Water that has been used by homes, businesses, farms or industry and requires treatment before being released into the environment.
Waste water from homes and businesses containing organic matter and harmful microbes, which must be removed before release.
The first stage of sewage treatment, in which large solid objects and grit are removed from the incoming waste water.
Allowing sewage to stand so that solids settle out as sewage sludge, leaving liquid effluent above them.
The settled solid produced by sedimentation, which is treated by anaerobic digestion.
The liquid produced by sedimentation, which is treated by aerobic biological treatment.
Breakdown of sewage sludge by microorganisms in the absence of oxygen.
Treatment of effluent by microorganisms supplied with air, so that they break down the remaining organic matter.
A rock containing enough of a metal compound to make extracting the metal worthwhile. The Earth's resources of metal ores are limited.
Rock that contains only a small percentage of a metal compound, too little for traditional extraction to be worthwhile.
Using plants to absorb metal compounds. The plants are harvested and then burned to produce ash that contains metal compounds.
Using bacteria to produce leachate solutions that contain metal compounds.
The solution produced by bioleaching, which contains dissolved metal compounds.
Obtaining copper from a solution of a copper compound by adding a more reactive metal such as scrap iron, which takes the place of the copper.

misconceptions.question: Water from the tap is safe to drink. Is it pure water?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is potable water, and potable water is not pure water in the chemical sense because it contains dissolved substances.
misconceptions.misconception: If water is safe to drink it must be pure, because safe, clean and pure all mean the same thing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday English 'pure' means clean or unspoilt, and bottled water is advertised as pure. Chemistry gives the word a much narrower meaning, met back in 4.1, that students rarely reconnect to drinking water.
misconceptions.correction: In chemistry pure means a single substance only. Evaporating tap water to dryness leaves a residue of dissolved salts, proving it is a mixture. Potable only means the levels of dissolved salts and microbes are low enough to be safe.

misconceptions.question: Does potable water have to contain no dissolved substances at all?
misconceptions.correct: No. It must contain sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and microbes, not none of them.
misconceptions.misconception: Water can only be called potable if every dissolved salt has been removed from it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students hear 'treatment' and assume the aim is total removal, and the word potable is often taught alongside purification.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says drinking water should have sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and microbes. Low is not zero; mineral water is potable and is sold on the dissolved salts it contains.

misconceptions.question: What do filter beds do to the water passing through them?
misconceptions.correct: They remove insoluble solids and larger particles. They do not kill microbes.
misconceptions.misconception: Passing water through filter beds makes it safe to drink because the filter traps the bacteria.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Filters are associated with 'cleaning', and students do not picture how much smaller a microbe is than a grain of sand.
misconceptions.correction: Filtration is a physical separation of insoluble solids. Microbes pass straight through, which is exactly why a separate sterilising step follows the filter beds.

misconceptions.question: What does the sterilising step remove from the water?
misconceptions.correct: Nothing solid. It kills microbes; the insoluble solids were already removed by the filter beds.
misconceptions.misconception: Sterilising is the stage that takes the dirt and grit out of the water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both steps are lumped together as 'cleaning the water', so their separate jobs are blurred.
misconceptions.correction: Each step has one job: filter beds remove insoluble solids, sterilising kills microbes. Chlorine, ozone and ultraviolet light do not remove any solids.

misconceptions.question: How is most potable water produced in the UK?
misconceptions.correct: By choosing an appropriate source of fresh water, passing it through filter beds and sterilising it.
misconceptions.misconception: UK tap water is made by desalinating sea water, because Britain is an island surrounded by sea.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Being surrounded by sea makes sea water feel like the obvious source, and desalination is the process students find most memorable.
misconceptions.correction: In the UK rain provides fresh water that collects in the ground and in lakes and rivers, so desalination is unnecessary. It is only required where supplies of fresh water are limited.

misconceptions.question: Can sea water be made potable by filtering and sterilising it?
misconceptions.correct: No. Filtering does not remove dissolved salts, so sea water needs desalination.
misconceptions.misconception: Sea water can be treated like river water; the filter beds will take out the salt.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat filtration as a general-purpose purifier and forget that dissolved substances pass through filter paper and sand alike.
misconceptions.correction: Dissolved salts are in solution, so they pass through any filter. Removing them needs distillation or a membrane process such as reverse osmosis.

misconceptions.question: How does the energy cost of desalination compare with treating fresh water?
misconceptions.correct: Desalination requires large amounts of energy, far more than filtering and sterilising fresh water.
misconceptions.misconception: Desalination is a cheap process because sea water is free and there is an unlimited supply of it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The raw material being free is confused with the process being cheap, and the energy needed to boil or pressurise water is invisible.
misconceptions.correction: Distillation must boil the water, and reverse osmosis must force it through a membrane at high pressure. The specification states directly that these processes require large amounts of energy.

misconceptions.question: In reverse osmosis, what passes through the membrane?
misconceptions.correct: Water passes through the membrane and the dissolved ions are held back.
misconceptions.misconception: The membrane's tiny holes let the dissolved salt pass straight through with the water, so membranes never really remove the salt.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'reverse' is read as meaning everything happens backwards, including which substance crosses the membrane.
misconceptions.correction: The membrane is a barrier that water molecules can pass but dissolved ions cannot, so pure water is collected on the far side and concentrated salt solution is left behind.

misconceptions.question: What makes a resource finite?
misconceptions.correct: It is not being replaced, or is replaced far more slowly than it is used, so supplies will run out.
misconceptions.misconception: A resource is finite if it cannot be recycled.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Recycling is the sustainability idea students meet most often, so it becomes the test they apply to every resource question.
misconceptions.correction: Finite is about the rate of replacement, not about recycling. Metals are recyclable yet the ores they come from are still finite, because no new ore is forming on a useful timescale.

misconceptions.question: What makes a resource renewable?
misconceptions.correct: It is replaced at the same rate as, or faster than, it is used.
misconceptions.misconception: Renewable means the material can be used again after it has been collected and processed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Renew' sounds like 'reuse', and re-using a bottle is a far more familiar act than re-growing a forest.
misconceptions.correction: Renewable refers to the resource being re-formed in nature quickly enough to keep pace with demand, for example a replanted crop. Re-using an object is a separate idea.

misconceptions.question: What does sustainable development mean?
misconceptions.correct: Development that meets the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
misconceptions.misconception: Sustainable development means stopping the use of the Earth's resources so that nothing is used up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sustainability is presented in the media as cutting back, so students hear it as a ban rather than as a balance.
misconceptions.correction: The definition has two halves: current needs are still met, and future generations are not prevented from meeting theirs. Development continues; it is the way resources are used that changes.

misconceptions.question: Is a cotton shirt a natural product or a synthetic one?
misconceptions.correct: Cotton is a natural product, obtained from a plant and supplemented by agriculture.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything farmed and processed in a factory counts as synthetic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Deliberate growing and industrial processing look man-made, so agricultural products get reclassified as synthetic.
misconceptions.correction: Synthetic products are made by chemical processes from other starting materials, such as polyester. Agriculture supplements natural supplies of a natural product; it does not turn cotton into a synthetic one.

misconceptions.question: Do sewage and industrial waste water need the same treatment?
misconceptions.correct: No. Sewage and agricultural waste water need organic matter and harmful microbes removed; industrial waste water may also need harmful chemicals removed.
misconceptions.misconception: Sewage and industrial waste water contain completely separate, non-overlapping contaminants, so each is assumed to carry only its own single type of pollutant - for example organic matter is taken to be only in sewage (so industrial waste has none) and harmful microbes only in industrial waste.
misconceptions.whyItArises: One treatment works is pictured as one process, and the contrast the specification draws between the two kinds of waste water is easy to skim past.
misconceptions.correction: The treatment matches the contaminants. Industrial waste water may contain harmful chemicals that domestic sewage does not, so it may require their removal as well.

misconceptions.question: Which part of sewage treatment happens without oxygen?
misconceptions.correct: Anaerobic digestion of sewage sludge. The effluent gets aerobic biological treatment, with air.
misconceptions.misconception: The sludge is treated with air and the effluent is digested without oxygen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two words look alike and the two products appear in the same sentence, so the pairing is memorised the wrong way round.
misconceptions.correction: Sludge, the settled solid, goes to anaerobic digestion. Effluent, the liquid, goes to aerobic biological treatment. Anaerobic means without oxygen.

misconceptions.question: What does sedimentation produce?
misconceptions.correct: Sewage sludge, the solid that settles, and effluent, the liquid above it.
misconceptions.misconception: Sedimentation produces effluent as the solid layer and sludge as the liquid running off.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are unfamiliar words learnt as a pair, and neither sounds obviously solid or liquid.
misconceptions.correction: Sediment settles, so the sludge is the solid at the bottom. Effluent is what flows out, so it is the liquid.

misconceptions.question: What does screening remove from incoming sewage?
misconceptions.correct: Large solid objects, and grit, which are removed physically at the start.
misconceptions.misconception: Screening removes the harmful microbes and the dissolved substances at the start of treatment.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The first stage is assumed to be the most thorough one, and 'screening' suggests checking everything.
misconceptions.correction: Screening and grit removal is a coarse physical stage that takes out rags, sticks and grit. Microbes and organic matter are dealt with by the later biological stages.

misconceptions.question: Which source is easiest to turn into potable water?
misconceptions.correct: Ground water, because it needs only filtering and sterilising.
misconceptions.misconception: Sea water is easiest because it looks clear and there is so much of it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Availability is confused with ease of treatment, and dissolved salt is invisible.
misconceptions.correction: Ease depends on what has to be removed. Ground water needs the least treatment, waste water needs more, and salty water needs desalination, which uses large amounts of energy.

misconceptions.question: A sample has 12 mg/dm3 of dissolved solids and sea water has about 35 000 mg/dm3. How do they compare?
misconceptions.correct: Sea water has roughly three orders of magnitude more, about a thousand times as much.
misconceptions.misconception: Sea water has about two or three times as much, because the numbers look fairly close on the page.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students compare the leading digits and ignore the number of zeros, so a factor of a thousand reads as a factor of three.
misconceptions.correction: An order of magnitude is a factor of ten. 35 000 divided by 12 is about 3000, which is three orders of magnitude, not three times.

misconceptions.question: In Required practical 8, where do the dissolved solids end up during distillation?
misconceptions.correct: They stay behind in the flask; the distillate collected is pure water.
misconceptions.misconception: The dissolved solids are carried over with the steam and collect in the distillate.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture everything in the flask travelling with the vapour, and do not separate boiling point from being carried along.
misconceptions.correction: Only water evaporates at the boiling point of the solution; the dissolved solids have far higher boiling points and remain in the flask. That is why the distillate has a pH near 7 and leaves no residue.

misconceptions.question: A water sample has pH 7. Does that show it is pure?
misconceptions.correct: No. pH 7 shows it is neutral. A neutral solution can still contain dissolved solids.
misconceptions.misconception: Any water with pH 7 must be pure water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Pure water is quoted as pH 7 in lessons, and students reverse the statement.
misconceptions.correction: Many neutral salt solutions have pH 7. Purity is tested by evaporating a measured volume to dryness and weighing any residue, not by pH alone.

misconceptions.question: What does phytomining or bioleaching produce directly?
misconceptions.correct: Metal compounds - ash from burning the plants, or a leachate solution - not the metal itself.
misconceptions.misconception: Phytomining and bioleaching give pure copper metal straight away.
misconceptions.whyItArises: They are called methods of extracting copper, so students assume the metal is the immediate product.
misconceptions.correction: Both methods produce metal compounds. The compounds must then be processed, for example by displacement using scrap iron or by electrolysis, to obtain the metal.

misconceptions.question: What do the plants used in phytomining take up from the soil?
misconceptions.correct: Metal compounds, which end up in the ash when the harvested plants are burned.
misconceptions.misconception: The plants absorb pure copper metal and store it in their leaves.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Plants absorb the metal' is a convenient shorthand that hides the fact that copper is present in the ground as compounds.
misconceptions.correction: The copper in the ground is in compounds, and it is compounds that the plants absorb. Burning the plants gives ash containing metal compounds, which are then processed.

misconceptions.question: What is the role of the bacteria in bioleaching?
misconceptions.correct: They produce leachate solutions that contain metal compounds.
misconceptions.misconception: The bacteria eat the rock and leave particles of copper metal behind.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Bacteria are pictured as consuming things, and the word leaching is unfamiliar, so the product is guessed at.
misconceptions.correction: The bacteria produce a leachate, a solution containing dissolved metal compounds. Copper is then obtained from that solution by displacement or by electrolysis.

misconceptions.question: Why are phytomining and bioleaching used?
misconceptions.correct: They allow copper to be extracted from low-grade ores as copper ores become scarce.
misconceptions.misconception: They are used on the richest ores because they give the highest yield of metal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Newer methods are assumed to be better in every way, rather than being a response to the good ore running out.
misconceptions.correction: The specification links them to low-grade ores, which contain too little copper for traditional mining to be worthwhile, and to avoiding the digging, moving and disposal of large amounts of rock.

misconceptions.question: Scrap iron is added to a solution of copper sulfate. What happens?
misconceptions.correct: Iron is more reactive, so it displaces copper and copper metal is produced.
misconceptions.misconception: Copper is more reactive than iron, so the copper displaces the iron from the solution.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Copper is a familiar, valuable metal, so students assume it must be the more reactive of the two.
misconceptions.correction: In the reactivity series iron is above copper. The more reactive metal goes into solution and the less reactive metal is displaced out, so iron dissolves and copper is deposited.

misconceptions.question: At which electrode is copper produced when a copper solution is electrolysed?
misconceptions.correct: At the negative electrode, because copper ions are positive.
misconceptions.misconception: Copper is produced at the positive electrode.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that copper is used as an electrode in the purification cell and lose track of which charge attracts the metal ions.
misconceptions.correction: Copper ions carry a positive charge, so they are attracted to the negative electrode, where they gain electrons and form copper metal.

misconceptions.question: What counts as one of the Earth's resources?
misconceptions.correct: Anything taken from the Earth, oceans or atmosphere that people use, including food, timber and clothing.
misconceptions.misconception: Resources means only the fuels and metals that are dug out of rock.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mining and drilling are the images attached to the word, so living and atmospheric resources are left off the list.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says humans use the Earth's resources for warmth, shelter, food and transport, and that natural resources, supplemented by agriculture, provide food, timber, clothing and fuels.

misconceptions.question: Can ultraviolet light sterilise drinking water?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Sterilising agents used for potable water include chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light.
misconceptions.misconception: Ultraviolet light cannot sterilise water because no chemical is added to it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sterilising is assumed to mean dosing with a chemical, so a physical agent does not look like treatment at all.
misconceptions.correction: The specification names three sterilising agents: chlorine, ozone and ultraviolet light. Ultraviolet light kills microbes without adding anything to the water.

misconceptions.question: Are the Earth's resources of metal ores limited?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The Earth's resources of metal ores are limited, and copper ores in particular are becoming scarce.
misconceptions.misconception: Ores will never run out because recycling keeps putting metal back.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Recycling is presented as the answer to resource shortage, which makes the original supply feel unlimited.
misconceptions.correction: Recycling reuses metal already extracted; it creates no new ore. The specification states plainly that the Earth's resources of metal ores are limited.

misconceptions.question: Is the same method used to produce potable water everywhere in the world?
misconceptions.correct: No. The methods used depend on available supplies of water and local conditions.
misconceptions.misconception: There is one standard treatment process used in every country.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A single treatment diagram is learnt, so it is taken to be universal rather than the UK case.
misconceptions.correction: Where fresh water is plentiful, filtering and sterilising is enough. Where fresh water is limited, desalination of salty water or sea water may be required.

misconceptions.question: Is timber a finite resource?
misconceptions.correct: No. Trees can be replanted and regrown, so timber is renewable.
misconceptions.misconception: Fossil fuels such as natural gas are still being formed slowly underground all the time, so they count as renewable and will not run out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The individual tree is the thing students picture, rather than the managed woodland that keeps replacing it.
misconceptions.correction: Finite and renewable describe the supply, not one object. Trees are replanted and regrow within a human lifetime, so timber is renewable, unlike crude oil.

misconceptions.question: Does sustainable development mean putting future generations first?
misconceptions.correct: No. It meets the needs of current generations as well, without compromising future ones.
misconceptions.misconception: Sustainable development means giving up what we need now so that future generations have more.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The phrase 'future generations' is the memorable half of the definition, so the first half drops out.
misconceptions.correction: The definition is a balance of both: current needs are met, and the ability of future generations to meet their own needs is not compromised.

misconceptions.question: A table shows that country A uses the least water per person. What can be concluded?
misconceptions.correct: Only that its use per person is the lowest of those shown; the table gives no reason for it.
misconceptions.misconception: The country using the least water per person must be the one with the driest climate.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students look for an explanation rather than a reading, and climate is the first cause that comes to mind, so a cause is read into a table that records none.
misconceptions.correction: Extracting information means stating what the figures show. A cause, a total or a future trend can only be claimed if the chart, graph or table actually contains that information.

misconceptions.question: Is water from a clean-looking lake safe to drink as it is?
misconceptions.correct: No. It must still be filtered and sterilised before it is potable.
misconceptions.misconception: Water from a clear lake or river is already potable because it looks clean.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Appearance is treated as evidence of safety, and microbes cannot be seen.
misconceptions.correction: Fresh water has low levels of dissolved substances but can still carry microbes. Choosing the source is only the first step; filtering and sterilising follow.

misconceptions.question: A table gives the water used per person per day in four countries. Does the largest figure show which country uses the most water in total?
misconceptions.correct: No. A total also depends on the population, which the table does not give.
misconceptions.misconception: The country with the largest per-person figure must use the largest total volume of water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The heading 'per person per day' is skimmed and the figure is read as a plain amount, so the biggest number is taken to mean the biggest user.
misconceptions.correction: A per-person figure is a rate. It would have to be multiplied by the population to give a total, and the table gives no populations, so no total can be claimed from it.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about how humans use the Earth's resources is correct?

options.text: Earth's resources provide warmth, shelter, food and transport
options.rationale: The specification states exactly this use of the Earth's resources.

options.text: Earth's resources means the fuels and metals dug from rock
options.rationale: Mining and drilling are the images attached to the word, so food and shelter are excluded.

options.text: Farmed crops count as synthetic and not as resources
options.rationale: Deliberate growing and factory processing make farmed products look man-made, so they are struck off the list.

options.text: Earth's resources supply transport but not warmth
options.rationale: Selects one item from the specification's list and rejects the rest of it.

mcqs.stem: Natural resources are supplemented by agriculture. Which list of products does the specification give for these resources?

options.text: Warmth, shelter, transport and heavy machinery
options.rationale: Confuses the uses of the Earth's resources with the products the specification lists.

options.text: Food, timber, clothing and fuels are all provided
options.rationale: The specification states that natural resources, supplemented by agriculture, provide food, timber, clothing and fuels.

options.text: Food and clothing only, since fuels are all synthetic
options.rationale: Assumes fuels must be manufactured, so they are struck off the natural list.

options.text: Only timber and other farmed plant materials
options.rationale: Narrows the list to what is obviously grown, dropping fuels and clothing.

mcqs.stem: Which pair correctly matches a natural product with the synthetic product that can replace it?

options.text: Natural cotton fibre is replaced by farmed wool fibre
options.rationale: Both are natural products from living things, so neither replacement is synthetic.

options.text: Natural rubber from latex is replaced by iron and steel
options.rationale: Names a real material but not one that replaces rubber in the same use.

options.text: Natural rubber from latex replaced by synthetic rubber
options.rationale: Latex tapped from rubber trees is a natural product and synthetic rubber, made industrially, supplements and replaces it.

options.text: Farmed timber is replaced by synthetic wood made from trees
options.rationale: Treats a farmed natural product as synthetic simply because it is processed.

mcqs.stem: Finite resources from the Earth, oceans and atmosphere are processed. What does the specification say this provides?

options.text: Renewable supplies that will never be used up
options.rationale: Contradicts the meaning of finite and confuses it with renewable.

options.text: Only fuels and metals dug straight out of the rock
options.rationale: Splits the two products of processing and assigns materials to agriculture.

options.text: Metal ores that are then recycled indefinitely by us
options.rationale: Recycling is added from elsewhere; it is not what the statement says.

options.text: Energy and the materials that people can use
options.rationale: The specification states that finite resources are processed to provide energy and materials.

mcqs.stem: What makes a resource finite rather than renewable?

options.text: It cannot be recycled after it has been used
options.rationale: Recycling is the sustainability idea students meet most, so it becomes the test they apply.

options.text: It is used up more quickly than it is replaced
options.rationale: A finite resource is not being replaced, or is replaced far more slowly than it is used, so it will run out.

options.text: It is buried underground rather than grown
options.rationale: Where it is found is not the test; some underground water is replaced by rain.

options.text: It cannot be used more than a single time
options.rationale: Confuses re-using an object with the resource being re-formed.

mcqs.stem: A student is given data on four materials. Which one should be classified as a renewable resource?

options.text: Copper ore, because copper can be melted and reused
options.rationale: Recyclability is mistaken for renewability; no new ore is forming.

options.text: Crude oil, because more is still being discovered
options.rationale: Discovery of existing deposits is confused with replacement of the resource.

options.text: Timber, because the trees felled are all replanted
options.rationale: Trees are replaced at a rate that keeps pace with use, so timber is renewable.

options.text: Natural gas, as it forms constantly underground
options.rationale: Formation over millions of years is treated as keeping pace with demand.

mcqs.stem: Which of these best describes sustainable development?

options.text: Development that uses none of the natural resources of the Earth at all
options.rationale: Sustainability is heard as a ban on use rather than as a balance.

options.text: Development that meets the needs of future generations rather than those of people now
options.rationale: Keeps the memorable half of the definition and drops the present-day half.

options.text: Development in which every material that industry uses is recycled afterwards
options.rationale: Recycling is one tactic, not the definition the specification gives.

options.text: Development that meets the needs of today without compromising future ones
options.rationale: This is the definition given in the specification.

mcqs.stem: What role does the specification say chemistry plays in the use of the Earth's resources?

options.text: It improves agricultural and industrial processes
options.rationale: The specification says chemistry improves agricultural and industrial processes to provide new products and contributes to sustainable development.

options.text: It replaces farming entirely with synthetic factory products
options.rationale: Over-reads 'new products' as the end of agriculture.

options.text: It removes the need to use finite resources at all
options.rationale: Sustainable development is misread as stopping resource use.

options.text: It is only useful once a resource has already run out
options.rationale: Treats chemistry as a last resort rather than an ongoing improvement.

mcqs.stem: A table shows the volume of water used per person per day in four countries. Which conclusion can be drawn from the table alone?

options.text: The country with the largest figure uses the largest total volume
options.rationale: Total use depends on population as well, which the table does not give.

options.text: The country using the least water per person has the driest climate
options.rationale: A cause is read into a table that records only volume per person.

options.text: The country with the largest figure uses more per person than the others
options.rationale: This is the only claim supported by a table of volume per person per day.

options.text: Water use per person is going to keep rising in every country
options.rationale: A prediction, not a reading; the table gives no trend over time.

mcqs.stem: A river sample contains 12 mg/dm3 of dissolved solids; sea water contains about 35 000 mg/dm3. How do these compare?

options.text: Sea water contains roughly three times as much
options.rationale: Comparing leading digits and ignoring the zeros gives a factor of three.

options.text: Sea water contains only about twice as much
options.rationale: Wrong: sea water (about 35 000 mg/dm3) is roughly three orders of magnitude (about 3000 times) more concentrated than the 12 mg/dm3 river sample, not a small multiple. A student who reads 12 and 35 000 as numbers that 'look fairly close on the page' underestimates the gap to about two or three times.

options.text: The two values are of a similar order of magnitude
options.rationale: Treats both as 'large numbers' rather than comparing them.

options.text: Sea water contains three orders of magnitude more
options.rationale: 35 000 divided by 12 is roughly 3000, which is a factor of about a thousand.

mcqs.stem: Why is potable water not described as pure water in the chemical sense?

options.text: Because it still contains some dissolved substances
options.rationale: Potable water contains dissolved substances, so it is a mixture and not chemically pure.

options.text: Because it has not been boiled before it is drunk
options.rationale: Adds a treatment condition that has nothing to do with chemical purity.

options.text: Because pure water simply means water that is clean and safe
options.rationale: Uses the everyday sense of pure instead of the chemical one.

options.text: Because a small number of microbes are always left in it
options.rationale: Sterilising kills microbes; it is the dissolved solutes that make it impure.

mcqs.stem: What does the specification say drinking water should have for humans?

options.text: No dissolved salts and no microbes whatsoever in it
options.rationale: Reads 'sufficiently low levels' as total removal.

options.text: Low levels of dissolved salts and microbes
options.rationale: The specification states drinking water should have sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and microbes.

options.text: Only water molecules, with everything else removed
options.rationale: Applies the chemical definition of pure to potable water.

options.text: Dissolved salts removed but microbes are left in
options.rationale: Splits the pair and drops the microbial requirement.

mcqs.stem: Why do the methods used to produce potable water differ from one country to another?

options.text: Because the same standard process is used in every country
options.rationale: Contradicts the question and reflects learning one diagram as universal.

options.text: Because sea water is the cheapest source in every country
options.rationale: Assumes desalination is cheap and always chosen.

options.text: Because some sources already look clean enough to drink
options.rationale: Treats rain-fed fresh water as automatically safe, so no other factor matters.

options.text: Because they depend on available supplies and local conditions
options.rationale: The specification states that the methods depend on available supplies of water and local conditions.

mcqs.stem: In the UK, what is the first step in producing most potable water?

options.text: Choosing an appropriate source of fresh water
options.rationale: The specification lists choosing an appropriate source of fresh water as the first step.

options.text: Desalinating sea water taken from around the coast
options.rationale: Britain being an island makes sea water feel like the obvious source.

options.text: Adding chlorine into the water at the source
options.rationale: Puts the sterilising agent first, before filtering and before the source is chosen.

options.text: Distilling sea water because supplies are unlimited
options.rationale: Distillation is a desalination route, not a UK first step.

mcqs.stem: Why is water passed through filter beds during treatment?

options.text: To kill the microbes in the water before it is drunk
options.rationale: Filters are associated with cleaning, and microbes are pictured as much larger than they are.

options.text: To remove the insoluble solids and large particles
options.rationale: Filter beds physically remove insoluble solids and larger particles.

options.text: To take the dissolved salts out of the water supply
options.rationale: Dissolved substances pass straight through a filter.

options.text: To lower the pH of the water before it is stored
options.rationale: Introduces an acidity change that filtration does not carry out.

mcqs.stem: What is achieved by the sterilising step in water treatment?

options.text: The grit and larger insoluble particles are taken out
options.rationale: Confuses sterilising with the earlier filtering stage.

options.text: The dissolved salts in the water are removed from it
options.rationale: Only desalination removes dissolved salts.

options.text: Harmful microbes present in the water are killed
options.rationale: Sterilising kills microbes so that the water is safe to drink.

options.text: The water becomes chemically pure and contains only H2O
options.rationale: Applies the chemical meaning of pure to treated drinking water.

mcqs.stem: Which set of sterilising agents for potable water is given in the specification?

options.text: Chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light are all used
options.rationale: These are the three sterilising agents the specification names.

options.text: Chlorine and ozone only, as light adds nothing
options.rationale: Sterilising is assumed to mean dosing with a chemical.

options.text: Sand, gravel and fine activated charcoal beds
options.rationale: Names filtration materials rather than sterilising agents.

options.text: Sodium chloride and dilute sulfuric acid
options.rationale: Plausible-sounding reagents that are not sterilising agents.

mcqs.stem: Which two methods of desalination does the specification name?

options.text: Filtering through sand, then sterilising it with chlorine
options.rationale: Applies the fresh-water route to salty water; filters do not remove salt.

options.text: Distillation, or a membrane process like reverse osmosis
options.rationale: The specification names distillation and processes that use membranes such as reverse osmosis.

options.text: Crystallisation of the salt, followed by sedimentation
options.rationale: Borrows separation words from elsewhere in the course.

options.text: Anaerobic digestion followed by aerobic treatment
options.rationale: Names the two sewage treatment stages instead.

mcqs.stem: The UK has plentiful rain. Why is desalination not used to supply most of its potable water?

options.text: Because sea water contains no dissolved salts in the UK
options.rationale: Factually wrong and would remove the need for desalination altogether.

options.text: Because membranes cannot remove salt from sea water
options.rationale: Reverses which substance the membrane holds back.

options.text: Because desalination requires large amounts of energy
options.rationale: The specification states desalination requires large amounts of energy, and rain supplies the UK with fresh water.

options.text: Because desalination is cheap but produces too little water
options.rationale: Treats the free raw material as making the process cheap.

mcqs.stem: How does the treatment of salty water differ from the treatment of ground water?

options.text: Salty water is filtered while ground water is only sterilised
options.rationale: Swaps the steps rather than identifying the extra process needed.

options.text: Ground water must be desalinated just like salty water
options.rationale: Reverses which source carries the high level of dissolved salts.

options.text: Both are treated in exactly the same way at the works
options.rationale: Ignores the dissolved salts entirely.

options.text: Salty water must have its dissolved salts removed
options.rationale: Ground water needs filtering and sterilising; salty water needs dissolved salts removed as well.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical 8, how is the mass of dissolved solids in a water sample found?

options.text: By measuring the pH of the water sample with a probe
options.rationale: pH measures acidity, not the quantity of dissolved solids.

options.text: By evaporating a set volume to dryness and weighing the residue
options.rationale: The dissolved solids are left behind when the water evaporates, so the residue can be weighed.

options.text: By weighing the distillate collected during distillation
options.rationale: Assumes the dissolved solids travel over with the steam.

options.text: By filtering the sample and weighing the filter paper
options.rationale: Filtration collects insoluble solids, not dissolved ones.

mcqs.stem: A student distils a sample of sea water in Required practical 8. What is collected in the receiving tube?

options.text: Salt solution that is more concentrated than before
options.rationale: Describes what is left in the flask, not what is collected.

options.text: Sea water with all of its dissolved solids in it
options.rationale: Assumes the dissolved solids are carried over with the steam.

options.text: Water that leaves no residue when it is evaporated
options.rationale: Only water evaporates and condenses, so the distillate is pure water and leaves no residue.

options.text: Water that must be pure because its pH is 7
options.rationale: Uses pH alone as a test of purity.

mcqs.stem: Why may industrial waste water need treatment that sewage does not?

options.text: Because it is always released straight into the rivers
options.rationale: Contradicts the requirement for treatment before release.

options.text: Because it contains no organic matter at all
options.rationale: Industrial waste water may still require removal of organic matter.

options.text: Because only industrial waste contains harmful microbes
options.rationale: Sewage and agricultural waste water are the ones needing harmful microbes removed.

options.text: Because it may contain harmful chemicals as well
options.rationale: The specification says industrial waste water may require removal of organic matter and harmful chemicals.

mcqs.stem: What is the purpose of screening and grit removal at a sewage works?

options.text: To remove large solid objects and the grit
options.rationale: Screening and grit removal takes out large solid objects and grit at the start of treatment.

options.text: To kill the harmful microbes present in the sewage
options.rationale: Assumes the first stage is the most thorough one.

options.text: To take the dissolved substances out of sewage
options.rationale: Screening is a coarse physical stage and cannot remove solutes.

options.text: To digest the organic matter without any oxygen
options.rationale: Names anaerobic digestion, which happens later and to the sludge.

mcqs.stem: What two things does sedimentation produce during sewage treatment?

options.text: Solid effluent at the base and liquid sludge above
options.rationale: The two unfamiliar words are learnt as a pair and swapped.

options.text: Microbes at the base and dissolved solids above
options.rationale: Wrong: sedimentation produces settled sewage sludge and the effluent above it, not separated microbes and dissolved solids. A student who believes the early settling stage removes harmful microbes and dissolved substances gives this answer.

options.text: Sewage sludge, which settles, and effluent above it
options.rationale: Sedimentation produces sewage sludge as the settled solid and effluent as the liquid.

options.text: Leachate solution and ash containing compounds
options.rationale: Borrows the products of bioleaching and phytomining.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the biological stages of sewage treatment is correct?

options.text: Sludge is treated aerobically and effluent anaerobically
options.rationale: The similar words and paired products are memorised the wrong way round.

options.text: The effluent from sedimentation is digested anaerobically
options.rationale: Loses the distinction between the two stages entirely.

options.text: The microbes are removed when the sludge is screened
options.rationale: Wrong: screening is a physical stage that removes large solids, not microbes, and it is not a biological stage at all; the biological stages are anaerobic digestion of sludge and aerobic treatment of effluent. A student who thinks screening removes the microbes treats it as the biological step.

options.text: Sludge is digested anaerobically and effluent treated aerobically
options.rationale: The specification lists anaerobic digestion of sewage sludge and aerobic biological treatment of effluent.

mcqs.stem: Rank waste water, ground water and salt water by how easily potable water is obtained from them, easiest first.

options.text: Ground water, then waste water, then salt water
options.rationale: Ground water needs only filtering and sterilising; waste water needs more stages; salt water needs desalination.

options.text: Salt water first, then ground water, then waste water
options.rationale: The size and clarity of the sea are mistaken for ease of treatment.

options.text: Waste water, then salt water, and ground water last
options.rationale: Assumes ground water is the dirtiest because it comes out of the soil.

options.text: All three of them are equally easy to treat
options.rationale: Ignores the different contaminants each source carries.

mcqs.stem: Why are new methods of extracting copper from low-grade ores being developed?

options.text: Because recycling means ore supplies can never run out
options.rationale: Recycling reuses extracted metal; it makes no new ore.

options.text: Because the copper ores left are becoming scarce
options.rationale: The Earth's resources of metal ores are limited and copper ores are becoming scarce.

options.text: Because low-grade ores give the highest yields of metal
options.rationale: Treats a newer method as better in every way.

options.text: Because traditional mining cannot extract any copper
options.rationale: Traditional mining works; it is the good ore that is running short.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes phytomining?

options.text: Bacteria break down the rock and leave copper metal behind
options.rationale: Wrong: phytomining uses plants that absorb metal compounds and are burned to ash - it does not use bacteria, and bioleaching bacteria produce a leachate of copper COMPOUNDS, not solid copper metal.

options.text: Plants absorb copper metal and store it in their leaves
options.rationale: 'Plants absorb the metal' hides the fact that copper is present as compounds.

options.text: Rock is dug up, moved and then disposed of in large heaps
options.rationale: Describes the traditional mining these methods avoid.

options.text: The plants absorb metal compounds and are then burned to give ash
options.rationale: The specification states that plants absorb metal compounds, are harvested and burned to give ash containing metal compounds.

mcqs.stem: What do the bacteria used in bioleaching produce?

options.text: Leachate solutions containing metal compounds
options.rationale: Bioleaching uses bacteria to produce leachate solutions that contain metal compounds.

options.text: Pure copper metal that is left behind in the rock
options.rationale: Bacteria are pictured as consuming rock and leaving metal.

options.text: Copper metal stored inside the plant leaves
options.rationale: Wrong: bioleaching uses bacteria, which produce a leachate of copper compounds; storing metal in leaves is a plant (phytomining) image. Bioleaching involves no plants, and the plants do not take up pure copper metal.

options.text: A copper oxide gas released into the air
options.rationale: Invents a gaseous product; no gas is named here.

mcqs.stem: Scrap iron is added to a solution of a copper compound. What happens and why?

options.text: The copper displaces the iron because copper is more reactive
options.rationale: Copper is familiar and valuable, so students assume it is the more reactive metal.

options.text: Iron displaces the copper because iron is more reactive
options.rationale: Iron is above copper in the reactivity series, so iron displaces copper from the solution.

options.text: Nothing happens because the two metals are equally reactive
options.rationale: Avoids the reactivity comparison altogether.

options.text: The iron is electrolysed at the positive electrode
options.rationale: Mixes up the two processing routes and the electrode charges.

mcqs.stem: A student compares phytomining with traditional mining of copper. Which comparison is valid?

options.text: Phytomining yields pure copper metal without further processing
options.rationale: The methods are called extraction methods, so the metal seems to be the immediate product.

options.text: Phytomining works best on the richest high-grade copper ores
options.rationale: Assumes a newer method must give the greater yield.

options.text: Phytomining avoids moving large amounts of the rock
options.rationale: The specification says these methods avoid digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock.

options.text: Phytomining removes the need to use any energy at all
options.rationale: Harvesting, burning and processing the ash all still require energy.

mcqs.stem: The table shows water used per person per day: W 60 dm3, X 95 dm3, Y 180 dm3, Z 140 dm3. Which statement matches the table?

options.text: Country Y uses three times as much water per person as W
options.rationale: 180 divided by 60 is 3, so Y uses three times the volume W uses.

options.text: Country Y uses about twice as much per person as country W
options.rationale: Y is compared with X, the next value in the table, instead of with W.

options.text: Country Z uses more water per person than any other country
options.rationale: Z has a large figure, but reading every row shows Y is larger.

options.text: Country X uses the least water per person of the four
options.rationale: W has the smallest figure; X is second smallest, not the least.
